reference.source: GeneReviews / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Troyer syndrome (SPG20) is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SPART, encoding spartin
It was first described in an Old Order Amish population and follows recessive inheritance, so a consanguineous or founder-population background may be a clue
The phenotype combines childhood-onset spastic paraparesis with dysarthria, distal muscle wasting, and short stature
Developmental delay, cognitive impairment, and emotional lability are frequently part of the picture
Skeletal features and a characteristic slowly progressive gait disorder help distinguish it from pure HSP
Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern supported by molecular confirmation of SPART variants
Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary, targeting spasticity, mobility, speech, and developmental support
reference.pathophysiology: Troyer syndrome shares the core hereditary spastic paraplegia mechanism of length-dependent degeneration of the longest corticospinal axons, producing lower-limb-predominant spasticity. SPART encodes spartin, a protein implicated in endosomal trafficking, epidermal growth factor receptor turnover, mitochondrial function, and lipid droplet regulation. Loss of spartin disrupts these processes within neurones, and the extensive functions of the protein are thought to underlie the additional developmental, cognitive, and somatic features that make this a complicated rather than pure form of HSP.
additionalDifferentials: Other complicated recessive hereditary spastic paraplegias (e.g. SPG11, SPG15)
Metabolic or lysosomal storage disorders with spasticity and developmental delay
Distal hereditary motor neuropathy when wasting predominates
additionalInvestigations: Brain and spine MRI to exclude structural causes and characterise any white-matter change
Molecular genetic testing of SPART, particularly in founder or consanguineous populations
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to assess distal wasting
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics presenting with spasticity and delay
redFlags: Regression of previously acquired skills suggesting a progressive metabolic or storage disorder
Rapid neurological deterioration inconsistent with the usually slow course
New seizures or focal deficits prompting reassessment
Feeding or respiratory difficulty from bulbar involvement in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: Troyer syndrome progresses slowly; many affected individuals remain ambulant into adulthood, though gait, speech, and cognition decline gradually and disability increases with age.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing static cerebral palsy in a child with a slowly progressive genetic disorder
Not recognising the founder-population context that raises the pre-test probability
Attributing short stature and developmental features to unrelated causes rather than the syndrome
Overlooking the need for coordinated developmental and rehabilitation support
management: Manage lower-limb spasticity with antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, and focal botulinum toxin injections where appropriate
Provide physiotherapy, gait training, mobility aids and occupational therapy to preserve ambulation and function
Offer speech and language therapy for dysarthria and swallow assessment as bulbar features progress
Support cognition and address emotional lability with appropriate psychological and psychiatric input
Manage distal wasting, contractures and skeletal features with orthopaedic and rehabilitation input
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive SPART variant, especially in founder or consanguineous populations
